procedural_history.originating_court: High Court (presumably Allahabad High Court, based on the parties involved)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Two orders dated 4 April 2023 and 19 April 2023 (referred to as 'Impugned Orders')
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State of Uttar Pradesh filed a recall application on 19 April 2023 seeking a recall of the First Impugned Order. The High Court also considered whether the power of criminal contempt could be invoked against officials of the Government of Uttar Pradesh on the ground that the application for recall was ‘contemptuous’.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court set aside both Impugned Orders dated 4 April 2023 and 19 April 2023 and disposed of the appeals. The High Court is at liberty to hear the writ petition, in view of the observations made in this judgement. The Supreme Court also allowed an amendment application and directed the petitioner to file an amended copy of the writ petition.

directions: Both the Impugned Orders dated 4 April 2023 and 19 April 2023 are set aside.
The High Court is at liberty to hear the writ petition, in view of the observations made in this judgement.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appearance of government officials before courts can be reduced to a routine measure, and whether they can be frequently summoned to exert pressure on the government under the threat of contempt.

facts: The case involved the conduct of a High Court, which was found to be frequently summoning government officials to appear in person.
These summons were often used as a tool to exert pressure on the government, frequently under the threat of initiating contempt proceedings.
law: The Supreme Court established that summoning a government official to court is not a routine measure and should only be resorted to in limited and exceptional circumstances.
The proper procedure is for courts to rely on the law officers representing the government (like the Advocate General) and the submissions made by the government on affidavit.
The Court's power to summon officials should not be used as a coercive tool to pressure the government.
This practice runs contrary to the constitutional scheme, which recognizes law officers as the primary point of contact between the judiciary and the government.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's conduct was impermissible. Instead of adjudicating the legal issues based on affidavits or hearing the arguments of the government's law officer (the Additional Advocate General), the High Court repeatedly and improperly summoned officials.
This bypassed the established legal channels and misused the court's authority.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the practice of routinely summoning government officials to exert pressure is impermissible. To prevent this, the Court framed a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) to be followed by all courts, which provides guidelines on when the personal appearance of an official is necessary and emphasizes that it should not be the first resort. This SOP aims to ensure consistency, restraint, and maturity in the functioning of the courts.

issue.issue_text: Whether a court should direct the presence of an official solely because the official’s stance in an affidavit differs from the court’s view.

law.text: A court should not direct the presence of an official solely because the official’s stance in an affidavit differs from the court’s view.
The appearance of government officials before courts must not be a routine measure and should only be resorted to in limited circumstances.
Courts should rely on law officers and submissions on affidavit as the primary means of interaction with the government, rather than summoning officials as a first resort.
The presence of an official may be directed when the court is prima facie satisfied that information is being withheld, suppressed, or misrepresented.

application.text: The Supreme Court established that a mere disagreement between the court's perspective and the position taken by a government official in an affidavit is not a sufficient reason to compel that official's personal appearance.
Instead of summoning the official in such a scenario, the court should proceed to decide the case on its merits using the existing records, including the affidavit in question.

The Court contrasted this improper basis for summoning with legitimate reasons, such as when it appears information is being deliberately withheld or misrepresented, which would justify directing an official's presence.

The Court criticized the practice of repeatedly summoning officials instead of engaging with the government's legal position as presented by its law officers or in affidavits, deeming it an impermissible use of the court's power.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a court should not direct the presence of an official solely because the official's stance in an affidavit differs from the court's view. In such cases, the court should decide the matter on its merits based on the existing records.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court had the power to pass the directions summoning the government officials in the impugned orders.

facts: While adjudicating a writ petition, the High Court frequently summoned officials of the Government of Uttar Pradesh and passed various orders, including the impugned orders.
law: The appearance of government officials before courts should not be a routine measure and should only be resorted to in limited circumstances.
Summoning officials repeatedly, instead of relying on the law officers representing the government or on government affidavits, runs contrary to the scheme envisaged by the Constitution.
A High Court acts beyond its jurisdiction under Article 226 by frequently summoning officers to expedite a matter or exert pressure on the government.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's conduct in frequently summoning government officials to exert pressure on the government, under the threat of contempt, was impermissible.
The High Court used its judicial powers to summon officers to "browbeat" the State Government and expedite the consideration of certain Rules.
This action was deemed to be beyond the High Court's jurisdiction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court did not have the power to pass the directions summoning the government officials, as this conduct was impermissible, contrary to the constitutional scheme, and an act beyond its jurisdiction.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appearance of government officials before courts can be reduced to a routine measure, and whether they can be frequently summoned to exert pressure on the government under the threat of contempt.
appellant_arguments: The framing of the issue itself, which was accepted by the court, represents the appellant's argument that the appearance of government officials should not be a routine measure or used to exert pressure on the government.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (High Court) argued that the summoning was not a routine measure but was necessitated by the specific conduct of the officials, whose attitude was described as 'contemptuous' and who were 'attempting to stall all the recommendations of the High Court'.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a court should direct the presence of an official solely because the official’s stance in an affidavit differs from the court’s view.
appellant_arguments: The framing of the issue, which the court accepted, reflects the appellant's position that a mere difference of opinion between the court and an official's affidavit is not a sufficient ground for summoning the official.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (High Court) justified the summoning not merely on a difference of view, but on the grounds that the officials' attitude was 'contemptuous' and their stand was 'not reflected from the record', implying the affidavit was unsubstantiated or misleading.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court had the power to pass the directions summoning the government officials in the impugned orders.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that 'The High Court did not have the power to pass the above directions' summoning the officials.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (High Court) implicitly argued that it did have the power, justifying its order by stating that the 'attitude of the officers of the Finance Department is not only contemptuous' and they were attempting to 'stall all the recommendations of the High Court'.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court, acting on its judicial side, lacks the jurisdiction to compel a State Government to notify rules proposed by the Chief Justice on the administrative side, particularly when the Chief Justice does not have the competence under Article 229 of the Constitution to frame binding rules for post-retiral benefits of former judges.
obiter: Merely because reference is made to a wrong provision of law while exercising power, that by itself does not vitiate the exercise of power so long as the power of the authority can be traced to another source of law.
Policymaking by the government envisages various steps and the consideration of various factors, including local conditions, financial considerations, and approval from various departments.
Rules proposed by the Chief Justice without competence, at best, amounted to inputs to the State Government, which was free to constructively consider their desirability.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's invocation of criminal contempt and the subsequent taking of government officials into custody was not warranted. The frequent summoning of public officers, who are performing their duties as part of the executive branch of governance, is not an appreciable practice and is to be condemned. Courts should not use the summoning of officials as a routine measure or a tool to exert pressure, especially when a disagreement arises from an affidavit; instead, the proper course is to allow the state's advocate time to respond to the court's queries.
legal_tests_applied: The court evaluated the officials' actions against the definition of 'criminal contempt', which is conduct that: (i) scandalises or tends to scandalise, or lowers or tends to lower the authority of, any court; or (ii) prejudices, or interferes or tends to interfere with, the due course of any judicial proceeding; or (iii) interferes or tends to interfere with, or obstructs or tends to obstruct, the administration of justice in any other manner.
why_respondent_won: The High Court's invocation of criminal contempt powers was found to be unwarranted as the facts of the case did not meet the necessary threshold for such an action.

The Supreme Court held that the High Court's practice of frequently summoning government officials is improper and should be condemned, stating that while a court can set aside an executive decision that fails judicial review, it should not resort to routine summoning.

The court advised a more restrained procedure: if a question arises that the state's advocate cannot answer, the court should record the doubt in its order and grant time for the state or its officers to respond, rather than immediately summoning an official.
policy_considerations: The public officers of the Executive are also performing their duties as the third limbs of the governance. The actions or decisions by the officers are not to benefit them, but as a custodian of public funds and in the interest of administration, some decisions are bound to be taken.

It is always open to the High Court to set aside the decision which does not meet the test of judicial review, but summoning officers frequently is not appreciable at all. The same is liable to be condemned in the strongest words.
